questions.passage:
A team of ecologists studied three neighborhood gardens after volunteers added native flowering plants. The team recorded mean pollinator visits per hour at each garden during the same two weeks in June and July, before and after the plantings. The ecologists concluded that the new plants increased pollinator activity at every garden.

Garden | Visits per hour before | Visits per hour after
Riverside | 12 | 19
Oak Street | 8 | 15
Pine Court | 10 | 16

______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the ecologists' conclusion?
options: Oak Street had the highest number of pollinator visits per hour after the plantings, with 19 visits per hour.
At Riverside, pollinator visits per hour rose from 12 to 19, which shows that native plants can increase pollinator activity.
Pollinator visits per hour increased by 7 at Riverside and by 7 at Oak Street, but decreased from 16 to 10 at Pine Court.
Pollinator visits per hour rose from 12 to 19 at Riverside, from 8 to 15 at Oak Street, and from 10 to 16 at Pine Court.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is that pollinator activity increased at every garden, so the strongest support reports the before-and-after increase for all three sites. The table shows Riverside rising from 12 to 19, Oak Street from 8 to 15, and Pine Court from 10 to 16. An option that mentions only Riverside supports the claim less completely, and the option that says Pine Court fell misreads the table.

questions.passage:
Text 1: In an essay, cultural critic Irene Valdez argues that digitizing local historical archives creates a misleading sense of access. According to Valdez, people may skim an online photograph collection without visiting the library or consulting the documents' context, so digital copies risk weakening public engagement with history.

Text 2: Reference librarian Owen Paget notes that his city's library began uploading maps and oral histories while also increasing weekend workshops. Visitors who browse the digital collection often request the original materials or attend sessions about neighborhood history, he reports. Digital access, in Paget's view, is most valuable when it draws people into deeper use of the physical archive.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 2 dismisses the concern in Text 1 by arguing that physical archives are no longer necessary.
Text 2 repeats Text 1's view that digitization necessarily weakens historical understanding.
The two texts disagree about whether libraries should collect maps and oral histories.
Text 2 offers a qualified response to Text 1 by suggesting that digital access can encourage, rather than discourage, engagement with historical materials.
questions.explanation: Text 1 warns that digitized archives may let people skim materials without engaging deeply. Text 2 responds by reporting that digital browsing often leads visitors to request originals or attend workshops, so digital access can deepen engagement. It does not reject physical archives or claim digitization necessarily weakens understanding.

questions.passage: The city's first bicycle lane was installed on a two-block stretch in 2018. Some shop owners worried that removing parking spaces would reduce sales. ______, a study by a local business association found that sales at nearby stores increased slightly in the following year.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Likewise
For example
However
Therefore
questions.explanation: Shop owners expected a decrease in sales, but the study found a slight increase. 'However' correctly signals that contrast.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The novel's intricate plot and its vivid descriptions of coastal Louisiana ______ readers who might otherwise avoid historical fiction.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: has attracted
attract
is attracting
attracts
questions.explanation: The subject is compound—'plot and ... descriptions'—so it requires the plural verb 'attract.' The singular verbs 'attracts,' 'has attracted,' and 'is attracting' do not agree with the compound subject.

questions.passage:
A public-health team surveyed 400 adults in a midsize city about their weekly exercise and sleep. The team concluded that adults who exercised regularly were more likely than other groups to get sufficient sleep; ______

Exercise frequency | Reported sufficient sleep | Total surveyed
Regular (at least 4 days/week) | 75 | 120
Occasional (1–3 days/week) | 80 | 160
Rare (less than 1 day/week) | 48 | 120
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the team's conclusion?
options: Occasional exercisers had the highest reported rate of sufficient sleep: 80 of 160, or 50%.
75 of 120 regular exercisers reported sufficient sleep (62.5%), compared with 80 of 160 occasional exercisers (50%) and 48 of 120 rare exercisers (40%).
Regular exercisers made up the largest share of adults reporting sufficient sleep, since 75 of the 203 adults who reported sufficient sleep exercised regularly.
Rare exercisers had the highest percentage of sufficient sleep, at 48%, because 48 of 120 adults reported sufficient sleep.
questions.explanation: The regular-exercise group had 75/120 = 62.5% reporting sufficient sleep, compared with 80/160 = 50% of the occasional group and 48/120 = 40% of the rare group. These rates support the conclusion that regular exercisers were more likely to report sufficient sleep. The option emphasizing the occasional group’s larger raw count is tempting but does not show the highest rate.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Historian Rafael Mendes argues that the federal mural program of the 1930s mainly projected a standardized image of national renewal. Because the program required approval from federal administrators, Mendes contends, artists tended to portray workers and landscapes in ways that minimized regional conflict and emphasized collective purpose.

Text 2: Art historian Clara Nwosu cautions against treating the murals as a single message. She shows that local committees often chose themes and that artists included details of specific industries, immigrant neighborhoods, and labor disputes. Federal officials approved the works, Nwosu notes, but local audiences and artists shaped what the walls actually depicted.
questions.q: Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that the mural program projected a standardized image?
options: Nwosu would agree that federal approval mattered but argue that local influence made the murals less uniform than Mendes suggests.
She would claim that Mendes's focus on regional conflict is irrelevant to all public art.
She would deny that federal administrators had any role in approving the murals.
She would argue that the murals were standardized because local committees had no influence.
questions.explanation: Nwosu acknowledges that federal officials approved the works, so she does not deny federal involvement. Her emphasis on local committees and specific regional details challenges Mendes's characterization of the murals as standardized; she would therefore see them as less uniform than he claims.

questions.passage: Many museums now digitize fragile documents to reduce handling of the originals. ______, they often keep physical access limited to researchers who can demonstrate a specific need.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: For example
In comparison
Nonetheless
To that end
questions.explanation: The first sentence states the goal of reducing handling of fragile originals. Limiting physical access serves that same goal, so 'To that end' is the logical transition.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The novel opens with a map that helps readers understand ______ fictional geography.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: theirs
their
its
it's
questions.explanation: The possessive should refer to the singular noun 'novel,' so 'its' is correct. 'It's' means 'it is,' and the plural possessive forms do not agree with the singular antecedent.

questions.passage: The first trial of the new vaccine produced encouraging antibody levels in all participants. ______, the researchers cautioned that the sample was too small to establish effectiveness.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Similarly
Nevertheless
For instance
Therefore
questions.explanation: The first sentence presents encouraging results, while the second introduces caution about sample size. 'Nevertheless' correctly signals that the caution is being offered despite the encouraging findings.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Neither the mayor nor the council members ______ willing to comment on the proposal before the public hearing.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: was
is
has been
were
questions.explanation: With a 'neither ... nor' construction, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. The nearer subject is the plural 'council members,' so the plural verb 'were' is required.

questions.passage: When the city installed a network of rain gardens along Walnut Avenue, the project's effects were not ______: runoff increased in one low block after a storm, but nearly every other block saw less standing water and fewer basement leaks.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: uniform
favorable
subtle
temporary
questions.explanation: The colon contrasts one block where runoff increased with nearly every other block where runoff decreased, so the project's effects varied by location; 'uniform' means the same in every case. 'Favorable' would incorrectly characterize the effects as wholly bad, and 'subtle' and 'temporary' are not supported by the contrast.

questions.passage:
• Before the new study-space initiative, the library averaged 40 student visits per day.
• After quiet study rooms and peer tutors were added, student visits rose to 110 per day.
• In a survey, 78% of students using the rooms said they stayed longer than an hour.
• Book checkouts remained about the same after the initiative.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize how the initiative changed students' use of the library. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The library added quiet study rooms and peer tutors so that students would have a place to study.
Although student visits rose, book checkouts remained about the same after the initiative.
After the library added quiet study rooms and peer tutors, average student visits rose from 40 to 110 per day, and most students using the rooms stayed for more than an hour.
In a survey, 78% of students using the new rooms said they stayed longer than an hour.
questions.explanation: The goal is to emphasize a change in students' use of the library, and the strongest choice pairs the large increase in daily student visits with evidence that students stayed longer. The purpose statement does not show an effect, the checkout comparison shifts focus away from study use, and the survey alone does not capture the increase in visits.

questions.passage: Marine biologist Lena Ortega hypothesized that juvenile sea turtles in the harbor use bright buoys as resting platforms during strong currents. A team tracked 30 tagged turtles for two weeks and found that they spent much of each day near the buoys, especially when current speed exceeded 1.5 knots. However, the buoys were located in the warmest part of the harbor, where the turtles' preferred food was most abundant. The observations therefore do not clearly support Ortega's hypothesis because ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the turtles spent less time near the buoys when currents were strong
the team tracked only 30 turtles during the study
the turtles may have gathered near the buoys to feed in the warm water rather than to rest
the buoys were too far apart for the team to observe all of them
questions.explanation: The passage provides an alternative explanation for the turtles' proximity to the buoys: the area around the buoys had abundant food. If the turtles were feeding there, their presence would not necessarily show that they used the buoys as resting platforms. The other choices either contradict the passage or introduce issues not shown to undermine the hypothesis.

questions.passage: When the town's only hardware store closed, residents expected long drives to the next town for basic supplies. Six months later, however, the empty storefront had become a cooperative tool library: members could borrow drills, ladders, and garden equipment for small annual fees. The library's volunteer coordinator reported that membership grew fastest among renters in small apartments, a group that often lacks storage for tools it uses only occasionally. This suggests that the tool library succeeded partly because ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: it offered access to equipment that many members could not easily store or justify buying
residents preferred to own tools rather than borrow them
the town still had a hardware store that sold tools at low prices
professional contractors in the town needed tools every day
questions.explanation: The passage specifically notes that renters in small apartments often lack storage for occasional-use tools, which helps explain why a borrowing service would appeal to them. The other choices contradict the passage or describe groups and preferences that the passage does not support.

questions.passage: The historian's account of the strike was deliberately ______: rather than assigning blame to either the mill owners or the workers, she described the wage cuts and the walkout side by side, allowing readers to see how each side's decisions had followed from its own pressures.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: exhaustive
equivocal
partisan
evenhanded
questions.explanation: The colon explains that the historian avoided blaming either side and presented both perspectives, so 'evenhanded' best captures her fair, balanced approach. 'Partisan' is the opposite, 'equivocal' suggests unclear or evasive language, and 'exhaustive' concerns completeness rather than fairness.

questions.passage:
• The town's pedestrian bridge was built in 1958; engineers rated its deck and railings fair in 2022.
• In 2023, a loosened railing section closed the crossing for three days for repairs.
• Nearby crossings add 0.8 miles to the trip.
• Many students use the bridge to reach the middle school.
• Replacing the bridge is projected to cost $2.4 million; maintaining the old bridge costs about $180,000 per year.
questions.q: The student wants to write an introductory sentence for a report explaining why the town should replace its aging pedestrian bridge. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The pedestrian bridge was built in 1958, and replacing it is projected to cost $2.4 million.
Maintaining the old bridge costs about $180,000 per year, while replacing it is projected to cost $2.4 million.
Many students use the bridge to reach the middle school, though nearby crossings add 0.8 miles to the trip.
Because the aging pedestrian bridge has shown structural wear and closures disrupt an important route for students, replacing it would improve both safety and daily access.
questions.explanation: The goal is to introduce reasons for replacing the bridge, and the strongest choice connects the bridge's structural problems and repair closure to the daily needs of students. The other choices provide isolated facts about cost, use, or maintenance without clearly arguing that replacement is needed.

questions.passage: Researchers hypothesized that the new after-school tutoring program improved students' confidence in math more than their math test scores. They measured both confidence survey scores and math test scores before and after one semester. Students' average confidence scores rose by 12 points, while their average math test scores rose by 3 points. To better evaluate this hypothesis, the researchers should compare these changes with ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the confidence scores of the program's tutors before and after their training
the number of tutoring sessions each student attended
the changes in confidence and test scores among similar students who did not attend the program
the average math test score of all students in the school before the program
questions.explanation: To judge whether the tutoring program caused the changes, the researchers need a comparison group of similar students who did not receive the tutoring. Session attendance might help study dosage, but it cannot by itself show whether the program had an effect; tutor confidence and a single pre-program test score do not provide the needed comparison.

questions.passage: At the community radio station, Nora volunteered to sort the incoming mail every Tuesday. At first, she simply placed pledge envelopes in one bin and letters in another. After a month, she began keeping a small notebook, recording the time each envelope arrived and whether it included a handwritten note. She noticed that envelopes with notes often arrived on Fridays, after the station's weekly volunteer shift. By spring, Nora had moved the Friday mail to the top of the station manager's stack because she believed that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the station manager preferred to open mail in the order it arrived
the Friday volunteer shift needed additional volunteers
the Friday mail was especially likely to contain handwritten notes that deserved prompt attention
most pledge envelopes arrived on Fridays
questions.explanation: Nora began tracking handwritten notes and found that they often arrived on Fridays, after the volunteer shift; moving that mail to the top suggests she thought those notes were important enough for the manager to see promptly. The passage does not support a claim that most pledges arrived Friday, and the other choices concern sorting order or volunteers rather than Nora's observed pattern.

questions.passage: A team of archaeologists studying a collapsed stone wall at a coastal site found that the wall's lower stones were encrusted with barnacles, while the upper stones were not. The team also found a layer of sand containing fragments of fishing nets on the inland side of the wall. The team concluded that the wall had once stood at the shoreline and that the inland area had later become a place where fishermen repaired gear.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the team's claim that the inland area later became a place where fishermen repaired gear?
options: The wall's lower stones contained barnacles, while its upper stones did not.
The site is located near the modern shoreline.
The fishing-net fragments were too small to identify the species of fish caught.
The sand layer containing fishing-net fragments was deposited before the wall was built.
questions.explanation: The claim that fishermen later repaired gear inland depends on the net fragments being from a period after the wall was built. If the sand layer and fragments predate the wall, they cannot show later repair activity. Barnacles support the shoreline claim, modern proximity is not decisive, and fragment size does not by itself undermine the claim of net repair.

questions.passage:
• The new pollinator garden was planted with native milkweed, coneflower, and goldenrod.
• During its first summer, volunteers documented 12 butterfly species and 9 bee species in the garden.
• A path with labels explains how each plant supports pollinators.
• In a visitor survey, 85% said the garden made them more interested in planting native species.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a nature center brochure that emphasizes how the new pollinator garden helps both insects and visitors. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The garden was planted with milkweed, coneflower, and goldenrod, and a labeled path explains each plant's role.
The pollinator garden provides habitat for at least 21 butterfly and bee species while its labeled path helps visitors learn how native plants support pollinators.
Eighty-five percent of surveyed visitors said the garden made them more interested in planting native species.
During its first summer, volunteers documented 12 butterfly species and 9 bee species in the pollinator garden.
questions.explanation: The goal is to emphasize benefits to both insects and visitors, and the strongest choice combines the documented pollinator species with the educational path for visitors. The other choices mention plants or a path, insects only, or visitor interest only, so they do not accomplish both parts of the goal.

questions.passage: In 2019, a neighborhood in Tucson began a tool library where residents could borrow drills, ladders, and gardening equipment instead of buying them. The library started with 60 tools donated by residents. Within two years, it had more than 400 items and 800 members, many of whom said the service helped them complete home repairs while saving an average of $120. The library also became a place where neighbors exchanged advice about repairs and shared recommendations for contractors. For its founders, the most important outcome was not the number of tools but the network of mutual help that formed around them.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A tool-lending program in a Tucson neighborhood provided practical resources and fostered community connections.
Most Tucson residents prefer to borrow tools rather than buy them.
The tool library was valuable mainly because it helped members save money on contractors.
A collection of donated tools grew quickly but attracted too few members to succeed.
questions.explanation: The passage's main point is that the tool library provided useful items and built a network of mutual help. The other choices either overgeneralize to all Tucson residents, misstate the specific savings mentioned, or contradict the library's growth and success.

questions.passage: A team of biologists studying a mountain meadow found that a small bee species nested only in patches where a certain wildflower grew. The bees did not feed on the flower; instead, their nests were built beside its stems, which provided a windbreak. When the team removed the wildflower from three test plots, bee nests in those plots fell by half, while nests in untouched plots remained stable. The researchers concluded that the wildflower's value to the bees came from its physical structure rather than its nectar.
questions.q: According to the text, what did the researchers conclude about the wildflower's value to the bee species?
options: It provided shelter for nests rather than food.
It supplied the bees' main source of nectar.
It helped the bees locate mates across the meadow.
It attracted predators that controlled bee parasites.
questions.explanation: The text says the bees did not feed on the flower and that nests were built beside its stems for windbreak; removing the flower cut nests in half. The conclusion is therefore about physical shelter, not nectar. The choice about nectar directly contradicts the passage.

questions.passage: In a study of public murals in three Rust Belt cities, a sociologist found that residents rarely described the murals primarily as decoration. Instead, many described them as evidence that a neighborhood had a history worth preserving. Even murals that depicted painful events, such as factory closures or displacement, were often praised for making those events visible rather than for offering comfort. The sociologist argues that the murals' main function is not to beautify vacant walls but to help communities narrate their own past.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Residents of Rust Belt cities generally prefer murals that celebrate pleasant events.
Public murals can serve as a way for communities to narrate and preserve their histories, even when the events depicted are painful.
Public murals are mainly intended to decorate vacant walls in Rust Belt cities.
Factory closures and displacement are the most common subjects of public murals in the three cities.
questions.explanation: The passage centers on the sociologist's argument that murals help communities narrate their own past, even when the history is painful. The other choices treat decoration as the main purpose, deny residents' positive response to painful events, or mistake examples for the passage's main claim.

questions.passage: In the early 1900s, public libraries in some US cities began offering evening classes for adults. These classes covered subjects such as bookkeeping, English, and civics. Library reports from the period often emphasized attendance numbers, but the numbers alone do not explain why the classes mattered. Many participants had left school early to work; for them, the library offered a second chance to learn skills that could lead to better jobs. The classes also gave immigrants and longtime residents a shared setting in which to discuss local issues.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence 'Many participants had left school early to work; for them, the library offered a second chance to learn skills that could lead to better jobs' in the text?
options: It explains why the evening classes were meaningful to many attendees, beyond what attendance data can show.
It compares early twentieth-century libraries with libraries today.
It challenges the claim that libraries offered evening classes in the early 1900s.
It introduces the paragraph's main topic by defining what evening classes were.
questions.explanation: The sentence explains why evening classes mattered: participants who had left school early gained a second chance at learning job-related skills. This goes beyond attendance figures rather than challenging the classes' existence or comparing past and present libraries.

questions.passage: For decades, engineers assumed that the shape of a bridge's arches was determined mainly by the strength of available stone. A recent analysis of 12 small stone bridges built in a mountainous region between 1870 and 1910 suggests otherwise. The engineers who built them varied arch shapes depending on local stream flow: wider, flatter arches were used where floods were common, even when the stone was strong enough to support a taller arch. The study does not claim that strength was irrelevant; rather, it shows that builders balanced structural concerns with the behavior of the water below.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall purpose of the text?
options: To explain how engineers today should calculate the strength of stone arches.
To compare small stone bridges with large modern bridges.
To describe a study that complicates a common assumption about why stone bridges were built with particular arch shapes.
To argue that stone strength played no role in the design of stone bridges.
questions.explanation: The passage describes a study showing that arch shape also reflected stream flow, not just stone strength, thereby complicating the older assumption. It does not claim strength was irrelevant or provide modern calculation instructions or comparisons.

questions.passage:
A city transportation department measured the share of commuters who used each mode of travel in 2018 and 2023. The data are shown in the table.
Mode | 2018 (%) | 2023 (%)
Bus | 18 | 22
Bicycle | 3 | 7
Car | 70 | 60
Walk | 9 | 11
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to describe the change in commuting between 2018 and 2023?
options: The share of bicycle commuters increased by 7 percentage points, and the share of bus commuters increased by 3 percentage points.
The share of bus commuters decreased by 4 percentage points, and the share of walkers decreased by 2 percentage points.
Car commuters made up more than three-quarters of all commuters in 2023.
The share of bicycle commuters more than doubled, while the share of car commuters fell by 10 percentage points.
questions.explanation: The bicycle share rose from 3% to 7%, an increase of 4 percentage points, and 7% is more than double 3%. The car share fell from 70% to 60%, a decrease of 10 percentage points. The bus and walking shares both increased, not decreased, and 60% is not more than three-quarters.

questions.passage:
Text 1: When Riverton converted six blocks of Main Street into a pedestrian zone, cafe owners reported more outdoor seating and a 15% rise in Saturday sales. The city’s planning office concluded that removing cars from the area helped small businesses draw customers who lingered downtown.
Text 2: Pedestrian zones can benefit businesses, but a team of economists studying a nearby city found that gains often depended on nearby parking and bus access. In the first year after a similar conversion, some hardware and grocery stores saw fewer customers who needed to carry heavy purchases home.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the planning office's conclusion in Text 1?
options: Pedestrian zones always reduce sales, so Riverton’s reported gains must be mistaken.
The rise in cafe sales shows that every kind of downtown business will attract more customers.
The planning office should have based its conclusion only on cafe owners’ opinions.
The conclusion may be too broad, since business gains can depend on transportation access and on the kinds of goods sold.
questions.explanation: The correct response reflects Text 2’s point that business effects can depend on parking, transit, and the goods sold, so Text 1’s broad conclusion needs qualification. A claim that every business will benefit overgeneralizes from cafe sales, and the idea that pedestrian zones always reduce sales is stronger than Text 2 supports.

questions.passage: The city's new overnight cooling shelters opened in July during a record heat wave. ______, many residents without air conditioning used the shelters during the hottest hours, and attendance exceeded organizers' expectations.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: In contrast
Nevertheless
For instance
As a result
questions.explanation: The opening of cooling shelters during a heat wave explains why many residents without air conditioning used them, so a cause-and-effect transition such as “As a result” is appropriate. “Nevertheless” and “In contrast” signal contrast, which the sentence does not contain, and “For instance” would introduce an example rather than a consequence.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The mural, along with several smaller mosaics commissioned for the same plaza, ______ installed after the community raised more than $18,000. Local donors said they wanted the artwork to honor the neighborhood's history.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: was
were
being
have been
questions.explanation: The subject of the main clause is “The mural,” a singular noun, and the phrase “along with several smaller mosaics” does not make the subject plural. Therefore, the singular verb “was” is required; “were” incorrectly agrees with the mosaics, while “being” does not provide a complete main verb.

questions.passage: A student claims that a town’s new recycling program works better when residents receive weekly reminders than when they receive monthly reminders. To test the claim, the student compares two neighborhoods of similar size and income. One neighborhood receives weekly reminder cards; the other receives monthly cards. After eight weeks, the student finds that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: both neighborhoods recycled more material than they had before the program began
the weekly-reminder neighborhood had more recycling bins visible from the street
the weekly-reminder neighborhood recycled 22% more material per household than the monthly-reminder neighborhood did
residents in the monthly-reminder neighborhood preferred the design of their reminder cards
questions.explanation: The claim is that weekly reminders work better than monthly reminders, so a valid support must compare the two reminder conditions. The result that the weekly-reminder neighborhood recycled 22% more material per household directly supports that claim, while a general increase in both neighborhoods or a preference for card designs does not isolate the effect of reminder frequency.

questions.passage: A team of materials scientists found that a new reflective rooftop coating reflected more sunlight than conventional dark roofing did. ______, in neighborhoods where many roofs were coated, afternoon temperatures were only slightly lower than in comparable neighborhoods with dark roofs, because heat stored in pavement and walls remained a major factor.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: For example
However
Similarly
Therefore
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes a coating that reflects more sunlight, which might be expected to cool neighborhoods substantially. The second sentence reports only slightly lower temperatures because pavement and walls still store heat, so a contrast transition such as “However” is needed. “Therefore” would incorrectly present the limited cooling as a consequence of the coating’s reflectivity, and “Similarly” and “For example” do not fit the contrast.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The oral history project that began with interviews of twelve retired shipyard workers ______ now includes voices from more than forty people across three generations. Organizers plan to publish excerpts online next spring.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: has expanded and
have expanded and
expand and
expanding and
questions.explanation: The subject of the main clause is the singular “The oral history project,” so the present perfect form “has expanded” is correct. “Have expanded” incorrectly treats the project as plural, “expanding” does not supply a finite main verb with “includes,” and “expand” does not agree with the singular subject.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Historian Elena Martinez argues that the Willow Park neighborhood, built in the 1920s, shows how readily Americans adopted the automobile. In her view, its wide streets and driveways were designed for cars from the start, and the neighborhood’s form therefore reflects car ownership.
Text 2: Maps from 1912 show that Willow Park’s street grid and lot sizes were planned before car ownership became common. Builders later added driveways, but the layout followed earlier streetcar-suburb designs. The neighborhood’s basic form, then, was not primarily car-driven.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Martinez's argument in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that driveways prove cars shaped the neighborhood’s original plan.
By noting that the neighborhood’s street pattern was planned before widespread car use, so its design cannot be attributed mainly to cars.
By arguing that wide streets made streetcars unnecessary in Willow Park.
By claiming that the 1912 maps were drawn after car ownership became common.
questions.explanation: Text 2 argues that the street grid and lot sizes were planned before car ownership became common, so the neighborhood’s basic form was not primarily shaped by cars. A response agreeing that driveways prove cars shaped the original plan contradicts Text 2, and the statements about streetcars and the date of the maps misstate the text.

questions.passage: In a review, drama critic Lena Ortiz claims that the new play The Blue Bench reveals the main character's isolation through the set design rather than through dialogue. Ortiz notes that the character speaks often and cheerfully to neighbors but ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: wears a blue coat that matches the color of the bench
always sits alone on a bench placed at the edge of a crowded stage
tells her sister a long story about a childhood vacation near a lake
spends much of the second act describing a dream about flying
questions.explanation: Ortiz’s claim is that isolation is revealed through set design rather than dialogue. The image of the character sitting alone on a bench at the edge of a crowded stage directly uses staging and set position to convey isolation, while the other actions are conveyed through dialogue or costume and do not as clearly support the claim about set design.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Each of the murals in the exhibit, which were painted by students from four different schools, ______ a short label explaining the scene. The labels will be printed in both English and Spanish.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: have
having
are having
has
questions.explanation: The subject of the main clause is “Each,” which is singular, even though the phrase between the subject and the verb contains the plural noun “murals.” The singular verb “has” is therefore required; “have” and “are having” incorrectly agree with the plural noun, and “having” does not supply a finite main verb.

questions.passage: A team of sociologists studying a neighborhood in Columbus, Ohio, hypothesized that block parties strengthen residents’ trust in one another. The researchers surveyed residents’ agreement with the statement “Most people in my neighborhood can be trusted” before and after a summer series of block parties. If the hypothesis is correct, ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: residents’ agreement with the statement rose more than it did among residents of a comparable neighborhood without block parties
residents who attended every block party had lived in the neighborhood longer than those who attended few
attendance at the block parties was highest during the first weekend of the summer
residents reported enjoying the block parties more than they had enjoyed the previous summer’s events
questions.explanation: The hypothesis predicts that block parties increase trust, so the strongest evidence would compare trust changes in a neighborhood with block parties to changes in a similar neighborhood without them. Greater enjoyment of the parties, longer residence among attendees, or high attendance during one weekend does not directly show an increase in trust or rule out other causes.

questions.passage: At the county historical society, archivist Lila Chen found two versions of a 1920s photograph of the same parade. In the first, the floats are crowded near the depot; in the second, taken minutes later, the floats have not moved, but several storefronts in the background appear closed. Chen noted that the photographer's notes list the time as 9:10 a.m. and mention that the parade was waiting for a delayed train. ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: The photographer's notes are unreliable because the floats did not move.
The parade organizers changed the route between the two photographs.
The storefronts remained closed throughout the entire parade.
The closed storefronts in the second photograph likely reflect that many businesses had not yet opened at that hour.
questions.explanation: The 9:10 a.m. time and the delayed train explain why the storefronts could still be closed moments later, so the closed stores likely reflect the early hour rather than a major change in the parade. The claim that the route changed is unsupported because the floats have not moved.

questions.passage: The reviewer complained that the documentary's treatment of the treaty was ______: it devoted only two minutes to decades of negotiation and skipped the competing claims of several nations.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: impartial
tentative
superficial
exhaustive
questions.explanation: The colon explains that the documentary gave very little attention to decades of negotiation and omitted competing claims, so its treatment lacked depth. Superficial captures that lack of depth; exhaustive is the opposite, and impartial and tentative do not fit the criticism.

questions.passage:
• Program: peer tutoring in math, twice weekly after school.
• Thirty students participated during the fall semester.
• Average math quiz score for participants rose from 68 to 75.
• Survey: 82% of participants said they felt more comfortable asking questions.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a school newsletter explaining how a new peer tutoring program helped students. Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: The program should expand to science next year because students enjoy asking questions.

By offering twice-weekly after-school math tutoring, the peer program helped participating students raise their average quiz score from 68 to 75, and most reported feeling more comfortable asking questions.
The peer tutoring program met twice weekly after school for students in math.
Thirty students participated, and 82% said they felt more comfortable asking questions.
questions.explanation: This sentence uses the relevant notes to show how the program helped: it names the tutoring format and reports both the score increase and the survey result. The other choices either state only logistics or recommend expansion without showing the program’s effect.

questions.passage: The museum's roof had leaked for years, and the staff had tried several temporary repairs ______ after a winter storm damaged two storage rooms, they finally moved the most fragile textiles to a climate-controlled room.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: : but
; but
but
, but
questions.explanation: The blank joins two independent clauses with the coordinating conjunction but, so a comma is required before it. A semicolon before but, no punctuation, or a colon before but does not follow Standard English punctuation conventions.

questions.passage: In a study of urban birds, a team of ecologists recorded the songs of sparrows at sites with different noise levels. At loud sites, the birds sang at a higher pitch; at quiet sites, they sang lower. When the team played recordings at quiet sites, resident sparrows responded more strongly to low-pitched songs, but at loud sites they responded more strongly to high-pitched songs. These results suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: high-pitched songs are always more attractive to sparrows than low-pitched songs.
sparrows' singing and responding are both shaped by the noise conditions in their surroundings.
urban noise has no effect on sparrow communication.
sparrows can learn completely new songs by listening to recordings.
questions.explanation: The sparrows sing higher where noise is loud and respond more strongly to the pitch that matches their noisy or quiet setting, so both producing and responding to song are affected by noise. The claim that high-pitched songs are always more attractive is contradicted by the quiet-site response.

questions.passage: The critic called the novelist's later work ______; rather than repeating the sprawling plots of her early books, she pared each story down to a few essential scenes, leaving readers to infer what had been omitted.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: didactic
ornate
spare
haphazard
questions.explanation: The context says the novelist pared each story down to a few essential scenes, so the later work is best described as spare or restrained. Ornate is the opposite, while haphazard and didactic refer to disorder or preachiness rather than concision.

questions.passage:
• Proposal: add protected bike lanes on Main Street.
• City survey: 63% of residents support the lanes.
• Data: storefront vacancies on Main Street rose from 9% to 14% over five years.
• Nearby city: after adding bike lanes, downtown foot traffic increased by 18%.
• Cost: $220,000, partly covered by a state grant.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a city council meeting that uses evidence to support funding protected bike lanes. Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: Because 63% of residents support protected bike lanes and a nearby city saw an 18% increase in downtown foot traffic after adding them, funding the Main Street lanes is likely to be both popular and economically helpful.
A nearby city added bike lanes, but some residents may prefer more parking on Main Street.
The proposal would cost $220,000, partly covered by a state grant, and local officials should decide whether to fund it.
Main Street storefront vacancies rose from 9% to 14%, and the bike lanes would cost $220,000, partly covered by a state grant.
questions.explanation: The sentence uses the strongest supporting evidence: resident support and the nearby city’s 18% increase in foot traffic, which together suggest popularity and economic benefit. The other choices mainly mention costs, vacancies, or an unspecified decision without making a case for funding.

questions.passage: After planting the seeds in moist soil and placing the trays under a grow light, the botanist had expected them to germinate within two weeks ______ the first sprouts appeared after nearly a month.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: but
, but
; but
: but
questions.explanation: The two independent clauses are contrasted with but, and a comma is needed before the coordinating conjunction. Putting a semicolon before but, omitting punctuation, or using a colon before but is not standard here.

questions.passage: Historian Ana Morales examined letters written by workers at a New England textile mill in 1911. The letters often mention long hours and low pay, yet almost none call for a union. Morales argues that this silence should not be read as satisfaction: many workers relied on mill-owned housing and feared that organizing would cost them their homes. ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Workers who did not mention unions were unaware that labor organizing existed.
Mill housing was popular because workers preferred living close to their jobs.
The letters prove that all mill workers were satisfied with their wages.
The absence of union complaints may reflect workers' economic vulnerability rather than contentment with their jobs.
questions.explanation: Morales argues that silence about unions may have come from fear of losing mill-owned housing, not from satisfaction, so the blank should state that economic vulnerability can explain the silence. The claim that workers were unaware of organizing and the claim that the letters prove satisfaction are not supported by the passage.

questions.passage:
• Project: restore a wetland behind Eastside High School.
• Students in biology classes will monitor water quality and collect plant data.
• The wetland filters runoff before it reaches the river.
• Local birdwatchers have recorded 14 species at the site.
• Cost: $18,000; volunteers will provide labor.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a grant proposal emphasizing the project's benefits for both students and the local environment. Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: Restoring the wetland would give Eastside students hands-on experience monitoring water quality and collecting plant data while also filtering runoff before it reaches the river.
The wetland already filters runoff before it reaches the river, and volunteers will provide labor for the $18,000 project.
The project would cost $18,000, with volunteers providing labor, and local birdwatchers have recorded 14 species at the site.
Eastside students in biology classes will monitor water quality and collect plant data at the wetland behind the school.
questions.explanation: The sentence connects a student benefit—hands-on monitoring and data collection—with an environmental benefit—filtering runoff before it reaches the river. The other choices mention only costs and species, only student activities, or only environmental work and volunteers.

questions.passage: In the 1960s, a group of Latina nurses in a Texas border city noticed that many families in their neighborhood delayed seeking care because clinics closed before most shifts ended. The nurses began holding evening sessions in a church basement, where they checked blood pressure, explained prescriptions, and connected residents to doctors. Years later, a public-health researcher interviewed the nurses and argued that their work mattered less for the number of patients seen than for showing how trusted neighborhood residents could fill gaps in formal health care.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The nurses' primary goal was to persuade local clinics to extend their regular hours.
The nurses' community-based evening sessions demonstrated the value of local trust in addressing gaps in formal health care.
The nurses avoided involving doctors in their work with neighborhood residents.
The sessions were considered successful mainly because they treated a large number of patients.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that the nurses' work mattered less for the number of patients than for showing how trusted local residents could fill gaps in formal care. The claim about treating a large number of patients conflicts with the researcher's point that patient counts were not the main measure of success.

questions.passage: Every Saturday, Mateo carried his abuela's battered record player to the front porch of their apartment building. He played boleros while she sold tamales to neighbors, and the melodies drew customers into conversations that lasted longer than the transactions. When a city inspector warned that the porch could not be used for business, Mateo worried the music would stop. Instead, his abuela borrowed a folding cart and moved the tamales to the sidewalk, where the record player, perched on a milk crate, kept drawing a crowd.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Mateo's abuela adapts her business while preserving the music that makes it a gathering place.
Mateo resents his abuela for ignoring the city inspector's warning.
The city inspector's warning ends the family's practice of selling tamales from the apartment building.
The record player is valuable mainly because it attracts customers who spend money quickly.
questions.explanation: The text shows the abuela responding to the inspector's warning by moving the cart to the sidewalk while keeping the record player and its gathering effect. The claim that the warning ends the practice is directly contradicted by her move to the sidewalk.

questions.passage: A team of marine biologists set out to learn why young oysters in a shallow bay were attaching to some rocks but not others. They first compared the chemical makeup of rocks where oysters clustered with that of nearby bare rocks. When the two types proved similar, the biologists turned to sound. They placed speakers near bare rocks and played the crackling sounds of a healthy oyster reef. Larvae settled on those rocks in much greater numbers than on silent ones.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It traces how a scientific question developed over several decades.
It presents a hypothesis and then describes an experiment that disproves it.
It compares two competing theories and concludes that both are equally supported.
It introduces a question, rules out one possible explanation, and then presents evidence for another explanation.
questions.explanation: The biologists ask why oysters attach to certain rocks, find that chemical differences do not explain the pattern, and then test sound as an alternative explanation. The settlement of more larvae near reef sounds supports that alternative rather than disproving it.

questions.passage: The first room of a museum exhibit displays ordinary kitchen tools from a 1920s farmhouse: a hand-cranked eggbeater, a dented colander, a wooden rolling pin. At first they seem too plain for a museum. The label beside them, however, notes that each was chosen because it was repaired at least three times. By treating mending as the objects' most important feature, the exhibit asks visitors to value not the tools' original design but the ingenuity and care that kept them in use.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the purpose of the last sentence?
options: It argues that original design is irrelevant to the history of household labor.
It suggests that the tools are too plain to be displayed in a museum.
It describes the specific repairs made to each tool.
It explains how the exhibit's emphasis on repairs changes what visitors are meant to appreciate about the objects.
questions.explanation: The last sentence explains the exhibit's intended effect: focusing on repairs directs visitors to value the care and ingenuity that kept the tools in use rather than their original design. The idea that the tools seem too plain appears earlier and is not the purpose of the final sentence.

questions.passage:
A team of transportation researchers studied a city's protected bike lanes. They counted riders on three streets during a weekday morning before and after planters were installed to separate bikes from cars. The results are shown in the table.
Street | Riders before | Riders after
Cedar Avenue | 120 | 156
Maple Street | 80 | 92
Riverside Drive | 150 | 210
questions.q: Which choice best describes the data in the table?
options: The total number of riders on all three streets increased by exactly 100.
Riverside Drive added more riders than either of the other two streets did.
Cedar Avenue had the largest percentage increase in riders.
Maple Street had the highest number of riders after the planters were installed.
questions.explanation: Riverside Drive added 60 riders, compared with 36 on Cedar Avenue and 12 on Maple Street. The total increase was 108 riders, not 100, and Riverside Drive's 40 percent increase was the largest percentage increase, not Cedar Avenue's.

questions.passage:
A public-health team tested four neighborhoods for the percentage of adults who reported walking for at least 30 minutes on a typical day. They also recorded whether each neighborhood had sidewalks rated as easy to use. The results are shown.
Neighborhood | Adults who walked (%) | Sidewalks easy to use?
Alta Vista | 34 | Yes
Brookfield | 22 | No
Cedar Park | 28 | No
Dunmore | 41 | Yes
questions.q: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the conclusion that easy-to-use sidewalks are associated with more walking?
options: Brookfield and Cedar Park had higher walking rates than both neighborhoods with easy sidewalks.
The two neighborhoods with easy-to-use sidewalks had higher walking rates than the two without them.
Dunmore had the lowest walking rate despite having easy-to-use sidewalks.
Walking rates were highest in neighborhoods with sidewalks that were not easy to use.
questions.explanation: Alta Vista and Dunmore, the neighborhoods with easy-to-use sidewalks, had walking rates of 34 percent and 41 percent. Brookfield and Cedar Park, without easy-to-use sidewalks, had rates of 22 percent and 28 percent, so the pattern supports the association.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Historian Daniel Cho argues that the expansion of streetcar lines in the early twentieth century created new suburban neighborhoods by making it possible for workers to live farther from factories. In his account, the streetcar companies often built amusement parks at the end of their lines to encourage weekend ridership, and housing soon followed those parks.
Text 2: Urban planner Renee Baptiste contends that streetcar suburbs grew mainly because lenders made long-term home loans available to salaried workers. Without affordable mortgages, she writes, even convenient transit would not have led families to buy houses far from their jobs.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Baptiste most likely respond to Cho's account?
options: She would argue that lenders built the streetcar lines themselves.
She would claim that streetcars made it impossible for workers to buy homes.
She would agree that amusement parks were the main cause of suburban growth.
She would argue that transportation improvements alone did not cause suburban growth; financing was the decisive factor.
questions.explanation: Baptiste says affordable mortgages were the main cause and that even convenient transit would not have led families to buy distant houses without them. This qualifies Cho's emphasis on streetcars and amusement parks rather than endorsing it.

questions.passage:
Text 1: A science journalist describes an experiment in which a team of biologists placed patches of native wildflowers along the edges of three crop fields. The team reported that the fields with the flower patches had more bees and produced, on average, slightly more fruit than fields without the patches. The journalist concludes that adding native flowers can help both pollinators and farmers.
Text 2: An agricultural ecologist notes that the experiment was conducted during one warm, wet season. She points out that in a dry year, wildflower patches might compete with crops for water and that the small fruit increase in a single season does not prove that the practice will always benefit farmers.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 2 rejects the data in Text 1 as fabricated.
Text 2 qualifies the conclusion of Text 1 by noting that the results may not hold under different conditions.
Text 1 and Text 2 agree that native flowers always increase crop yields.
Text 1 criticizes the methods described in Text 2.
questions.explanation: Text 2 does not deny the reported results; it warns that one warm, wet season and a small increase are not enough to show that the practice always benefits farmers. That makes it a qualification of Text 1's broader conclusion.
